description: I’m a solo developer participating for the experience and out of a genuine interest in space and technology.
summary:
Red Dust: Jezero Outpost is an interactive, browser-based game that puts children in charge of a Mars outpost. Players make decisions about limited resources while balancing crew survival with exploration and scientific discovery. The project addresses the challenge by turning space-survival concepts into choices players can experience. Instead of simply reading about mission constraints, children explore how using resources for one goal can leave fewer available for another. This makes planning, prioritization, and the consequences of decisions central to learning.

The project aims to bridge the gap between space education and engaging gameplay. By making the player a decision-maker rather than a spectator, it helps young learners understand that space exploration depends not only on rockets and technology, but also on thoughtful teamwork and resource management.
details:
What it does and how it works. Red Dust: Jezero Outpost is a free browser game for 7–12 year-olds who run a small Mars outpost. Three meters — power, air and radiation dose — plus two crew tasks a day are shared across seven jobs: make air, run the lab, drive the rover, grow food, send finds home, shelter from a storm, pile a soil berm. Nothing is free: the oxygen plant spends the same solar power the science needs, and a rover trip costs 0.3 mSv on top of the 0.64 mSv of an ordinary Mars day. Missions last 7, 14 or 21 days across four scenarios, with three goals: send finds, harvest crops, stay under the dose limit. Weather comes from ten real, dated NASA records — the May 2024 solar storm measured by RAD, the 2018 dust storm that ended Opportunity, InSight's M4.7 marsquake, Ingenuity's flights and more — shuffled by a seed. Every card names its source and says which effects are measured and which are game values. The forecast and the day's result come from one deterministic function, so the game cannot mislead.

Benefits and impact. Radiation becomes a budget a child can see and spend rather than an abstract fact. Players finish able to explain why sheltering costs the science, and why a longer mission is harder. It needs no account, install, network or personal data, so it runs on a shared school laptop or a phone; a mission fits a 20-minute lesson and scales from one week to three. The aim is a classroom-ready lesson built on real numbers, and a template for turning other NASA datasets into playable decisions.

Tools. TypeScript, React 18, Vite 5, HTML5/CSS3/SVG, Vitest (28 tests), Node 20 and npm, the Web Speech API for read-aloud, localStorage for saves. A static site with no backend or runtime API calls, hosted on Cloudflare Workers and deployed with GitHub Actions. No hardware beyond a browser. An AI coding agent was used and is declared on the project page, in the README, in page metadata and with a visible mark on the artwork.

Creativity and the factors we weighed. Creativity: no free "safe" choices; radiation as a budget rather than an alarm; a forecast produced by the same function that resolves the day, so planning beats luck; ten real events shuffled so replays cost no extra content. We weighed accuracy and provenance, reading age, fairness (an autopilot must win all 24 mission/setting/length combinations), accessibility (44–48 px targets, read-aloud, reduced motion), privacy, offline classrooms, low-end hardware, and the rules on NASA branding and AI disclosure.
